topic: Working With AI Feels More Like Leadership Than Coding
research_method: Web search (multi-backend) for discovery, then direct source extraction via web_extract on primary sources: metr.org study page, NBER Research Digest for WP 33662, arXiv 2609.24234 abstract page, Microsoft 2026 Work Trend Index report page + PDF, Faros AI blog + telemetry PDF, DORA 2025 report pages, Addy Osmani post. Vendor report (Anthropic 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report) verified only secondhand across 5+ independent outlets since the primary PDF is not publicly hosted. No browser rendering used; no curl/API failures encountered.
summary: The claim in the title is now empirically testable, and the evidence is more interesting than the metaphor. A NBER working paper (Weidmann/Xu/Deming, WP 33662) found that a leader's performance managing AI agents correlates rho=0.81 with their performance managing human teams (rho=0.69 after controlling for hard skills) - i.e. agent-wrangling is measuring real leadership skill, not a coding skill in disguise. Meanwhile Anthropic's 2026 report finds developers use AI in ~60% of their work but can fully delegate only 0-20% of tasks, and METR's RCT found experienced devs were 19% SLOWER with AI while believing they were 20% faster. So the article's spine is: yes, the job is now management - but management skill is exactly what prevents the two dominant failure modes (the delegation gap and the verification collapse). The practical payoff is that the management canon (Grove's task-relevant maturity, Management 3.0 delegation levels, Fournier's director model, decision rights) maps onto agents almost without translation, and the supervision loop is now documented (7 stages from arXiv 2609.24234).
verification_notes: METR 19% slowdown + 24%/20% perception gap: verified directly on metr.org study page (extracted). Paper: arXiv 2507.09089. Corroborated by Reuters, The Register, Business Insider.
NBER WP 33662 (rho=0.81 / 0.69, 0.65 SD, $23 vs $114, plural pronouns): verified directly on NBER Research Digest page (extracted).

Faros AI 2025 telemetry (+21% tasks, +98% merged PRs, +91% review time, +154% PR size, +9% bugs, no org-level DORA gain): verified in Faros' own July 2025 report PDF text (extracted snippet) and echoed by 4 independent sources. Faros 2026 dataset (+441% median review time, +31% PRs merged unreviewed, 25% AI-reviewed PRs) is from Faros' 2026 blog - single-vendor dataset, flagged as such in the article.

Anthropic 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report (60% usage / 0-20% full delegation / 27% net-new work / session length 4min->23min / multi-file edits 34%->78% / 47 tool calls / Rakuten 7h-99.9% / TELUS 13k+ solutions / Zapier 89% & 800+ agents): SECONDHAND. Corroborated across 5+ independent outlets (NYU Shanghai RITS, blockchain.news, danilchenko.dev, paperclipped.de, faq.com.tw). Do not present these as first-party-verified numbers; attribute to the report.

arXiv 2609.24234 seven supervision stages (Plan, Monitor, Wait, Review, Teach, Manual Fix, Update Assets; 19 experienced devs): verified on the arXiv abstract page (extracted). The stage names come from the paper's Figure 1 caption as quoted in the PDF search result.

DORA 2025 (90% adoption, >80% perceived productivity gain, 30% low/no trust): verified in Google Cloud announcement + Thoughtworks-hosted report PDF text. DORA 2024 (-1.5% throughput / +7.2% instability per +25% AI adoption) quoted from the 2025 report citing 2024.

Microsoft 2026 Work Trend Index (20,000 knowledge workers, 10 markets, Feb-Apr 2026; manager modeling -> +17pt value, +22pt critical thinking, +30pt trust; psychological safety -> up to +20pt readiness, 1.4x high-frequency agentic users): verified in the report PDF text (extracted).

CooperBench (50% lower success collaborating, 25% two-agent success, 26/32/42% failure split), JetBrains ICSE 2026 (14x delete/undo rework), OpenAI Codex concurrency telemetry (28.6% peaked at 5+ agents, p99 ~71 agent-hours/day), Bun 64-agent case, Cursor VCS conflict counts, Google Research 180-config sweep (+81%/-70%), Anthropic Claude Code concurrency caps: all SECONDHAND from secondary write-ups (Zylos, howardism.dev, Faros blog, latestagentic.dev). Use as corroborating colour, attribute loosely ('reported'), never as headline load-bearing numbers.

competitors.title: Your AI coding agents need a manager - Addy Osmani
key_points: Thesis: tech-lead/manager skills translate directly; 'AI coding at scale stops being a prompting problem and becomes a management problem.'
Two modes: local high-touch (architecture, taste, ambiguity) vs cloud/background async bounded tasks.
Frames a three-way split from OpenAI's AI-native engineering guide: delegate / review / own - engineers keep final sign-off.
Calls the real bottleneck 'should we build this?' and 'can I manage multiple agents?'; cites Boris Cherny running 5 local + 5-10 browser Claude Code sessions.
Warns about the over-delegation trap (product intent, API design, architecture, maintenance calls) and recommends WIP limits + kill criteria.
Parallel agents touching adjacent code = boundary failure, not tooling failure; git worktrees are the fix.

competitors.title: Managing Agents Is Management - Brian Conn
key_points: Strongest framing of the canon-transfer argument: agentic engineering is people reinventing normal management practice without knowing the literature exists.
Maps Andy Grove's Task-Relevant Maturity (1983) onto agent autonomy: trust is earned per problem class, not granted globally.
Maps Management 3.0's seven delegation levels (Tell/Sell/Consult/Agree/Advise/Inquire/Delegate) onto harness permission modes (plan mode = Consult, auto-accept = Advise, bypass = Delegate).
Decision rights: a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md is 'a decision-rights document for a worker with no judgment of its own' - defaults plus escalation paths.
Camille Fournier's director model -> invest a third of your time in guardrail/tooling authorship, not per-artifact oversight.
Cites MIT Feb 2026 working paper (Catalini et al.): the binding constraint is human verification bandwidth, not intelligence.

competitors.title: To Scale AI Agents Successfully, Think of Them Like Team Members - HBR
key_points: Deploying agents is not a software install but a change to how work gets done.
Enterprise framing: accountability, governance, and process redesign follow from treating agents as team members.
Useful as the 'this is an org-design problem, not a tooling problem' authoritative citation.

competitors.title: Leading all the AI agents and bots whose work you'll be accountable for - Fortune
key_points: Cites Harvard's David Deming research linking agent-coordination skill to human team-leadership skill.
Microsoft's 'agent boss' framing: onboard AIs like new hires, compose teams, set expectations, monitor early output, trust-but-verify.
Key inversion: with AI teams the human is more like an orchestral conductor than a jazz-ensemble leader - all coordination is centralized.
Five leadership skills: team composition/role clarity, delegation and task design, trust calibration, ethical oversight.
Charisma does not work on agents; you need prompt construction, error-pattern and model-capability fluency.

competitors.title: The code got cheap this year. The supervision didn't.
key_points: 'The code got cheap this year. The supervision didn't.' - the clearest one-line thesis for the review-bottleneck half of this article.
Autocomplete became delegation: the unit of work changed from accepting a completion to handing over a ticket.
Concrete remediation list: checks the agent runs before you look; review in a context that did not write the code; diffs in one keystroke.
Fleet guidance: three scoped agents with real file ownership beat six sharing a checkout; working limit 3-5 (roughly what you can review).
'Do not run a fleet without a check' / 'You are the queue' - the anti-pattern catalogue.

competitors.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity - METR
key_points: The essential counterweight to every 'agents make you a manager' post: the management instinct is measurably miscalibrated.
16 experienced devs, 246 real issues, repos averaging 22k+ stars and 1M+ lines; AI-allowed tasks took 19% LONGER.
Forecast +24% speedup; post-hoc belief +20% speedup; actual -19%. Perception and reality are inversely signed.

Five contributing factors: over-optimism about AI usefulness, high developer familiarity with the repo, large/complex repos, low AI reliability (<44% of suggestions accepted then cleaned up), implicit repository context.
Authors explicitly scope the result: it does NOT show AI fails to speed up most developers; other settings (unfamiliar code, less experienced devs, new projects) plausibly differ.

competitors.title: Multi-Agent Software Development: AI-Native Engineering Teams in Practice - Zylos Research
key_points: Role taxonomy that recurs across production systems: Coordinator/Lead, Developer/Builder, Reviewer, QA/Tester, Architect/Planner, Researcher.
Communication patterns: hub-and-spoke, peer-to-peer, shared task list, structured documents, broadcast, file-reservation leases.
CooperBench (Jan 2026): agents achieve ~50% lower success collaborating than solo; two-agent cooperation only 25% success; failure split comms 26% / commitment 32% / expectation 42%.
'Agentic drift' - parallel agents converge on conflicting implementations of the same concept while tests still pass.
Production failure breakdown: specification 41.8%, coordination 36.9%, verification 21.3%.

competitors.title: Parallel Agent Orchestration - howardism.dev
key_points: OpenAI Codex telemetry: 28.6% of staff peaked at 5+ concurrent agents; p99 ~71 agent-hours/day - hard numbers for the role inversion.
Frames the inversion explicitly: the human stops being executor and becomes delegator-monitor-reviewer-coordinator.

Bun's 64-Claude Zig->Rust port: shared-tree agents destroyed each other within minutes (git stash/reset incidents); worktree-per-agent rejected on disk grounds; 4-worktree sharding; systemd-run cgroup isolation.

Cursor rebuilt version control from scratch: >70,000 merge conflicts before a pause, hottest single file hit 7,771 conflicts from 1,173 distinct agents; after the rebuild <1,000 conflicts and 47 on the worst file.
Claude Code concurrency caps shipped as defaults (200 subagents/session, 20 concurrent, 'fewer than 15 agents' workflow guideline) - vendor acknowledging runaway delegation.

competitors.title: Leadership Skills: Managing AI Agents vs. Humans - NBER Research Digest
key_points: The single strongest evidence that 'working with AI is leadership' is not just a metaphor: rho=0.81 between AI-agent leadership and human-team leadership performance.
rho=0.69 after controlling for hard skills (task-specific ability, fluid intelligence) - the AI task is capturing leadership-specific soft skills.
Leader quality explained >half the variation in team performance in both settings; +1 SD leader -> ~+0.65 SD team performance.
Behavioural markers of successful leaders in BOTH settings: more questions, more conversational turn-taking, more plural pronouns ('we'/'us').
Economics: AI-based measurement $23/participant vs $114 for the human version, and no multi-participant scheduling.

angles: SPINE: The title is now a testable claim, not a vibe. NBER WP 33662 shows managing AI agents is a valid proxy for measuring real human leadership skill (rho=0.81) - the strongest available evidence that this shift is genuinely a promotion into management, and that the skill is transferable in both directions.

THE TRAP: But the same literature shows management instinct is miscalibrated by default - METR's developers were 19% slower while insisting they were 20% faster. Leadership without measurement is how you get a confident, wrong fleet. This is the article's tension: you are a manager now, and the first management skill is honest instrumentation.
THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: The delegation gap - 60% AI usage, 0-20% full delegation. Frame it as trust calibration (per problem class, per Grove's task-relevant maturity), not as a model-capability gap.

THE BINDING CONSTRAINT: Verification bandwidth, not generation. Faros' review-time blow-up (+91% -> +441%), the 31% of PRs now merging with zero review, and the MIT 'verification bandwidth' framing. The article can argue: your fleet size is a review-capacity decision, not a model decision.

THE CANON REFRAME (unique angle): you are not inventing a new discipline, you are rediscovering management - Grove (1983), Management 3.0 delegation poker, Fournier's director model, decision rights. Harness permission modes literally implement the delegation spectrum. This is the 'you already know this, go read the literature' payoff.

THE OPERATIONAL MODEL: The 7-stage supervision loop (Plan, Monitor, Wait, Review, Teach, Manual Fix, Update Assets) from arXiv 2609.24234 - gives the guide a defensible process diagram instead of generic advice, and explains why 'Update Assets' (turning recurring guidance into reusable artifacts) is the compounding lever.

THE ANTI-HYPE SECTION: When NOT to run a fleet - sequential/critical-path work (-70% on Google's sequential benchmark; CooperBench ~50% lower success collaborating), shared files, small tasks (negative ROI below ~30 min), and over-delegation of judgment work ('should we build this?').

PERSONAL COST ANGLE: the 'senior engineer tax' - 25% of PRs are now agent-reviewed and review time still nearly doubled; 31% of PRs merge unreviewed; JetBrains' 14x delete/undo rework. Reviewers are the new bottleneck and nobody budgets for that headcount.

faq.q: Why does working with AI coding agents feel like leadership instead of coding?
faq.a: Because the unit of work changed from writing code to delegating and verifying it (Anthropic 2026: AI in ~60% of work, but only 0-20% fully delegated), and the skills involved - decomposition, expectation-setting, trust calibration, review - are the same skills that predict success managing human teams (NBER WP 33662: rho=0.81).

faq.q: Is managing AI agents really the same skill as managing people?
faq.a: The strongest evidence says the overlap is large but not total: rho=0.81 raw, rho=0.69 after controlling for hard skills. What does NOT transfer: agents do not negotiate roles, self-organize or provide psychological safety, so coordination stays centralized on the human - closer to a conductor than a jazz-ensemble leader.

faq.q: How many AI coding agents should one developer manage?
faq.a: Bound it by review capacity, not model capacity. Practitioner ceilings cluster at 3-5 concurrently for meaningful work, 5-7 for CLI agents on a laptop before rate limits and merge conflicts bite, and Anthropic's own harness ships a 20-concurrent default with a 'fewer than 15 agents' guideline. If nobody is reviewing, the fleet is generating obligations, not value.

faq.q: How do I know which tasks to fully delegate?
faq.a: Use delegation levels rather than a binary: plan mode ≈ Consult, auto-accept ≈ Advise, full bypass ≈ Delegate. Delegate mechanical, crisply specified, independently testable work. Keep ownership of product intent, architecture, shared interfaces, security-sensitive changes and 'should we build this?' decisions. Raise autonomy per task class only after that class earns it (Grove's task-relevant maturity).

Anthropic's 2026 report found developers use AI in ~60% of their work but report being able to fully delegate only 0-20% of tasks without line-by-line review. It is a trust and verification problem: closing it requires automated evaluation, clear escalation rules and evidence standards, not just better models.

faq.q: What should I track to know agentic coding is actually working?
faq.a: Not PR count. Track verification-side metrics: time in review, PR size, share of PRs merged with no review, rework (undo/delete churn), escaped bugs and incidents per PR. Faros' 2026 telemetry shows exactly why: outputs up, median time in PR review up 441%, and 31% more PRs merging with no review at all.

faq.q: Where do I put the rules I want every agent to follow?
faq.a: Treat AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md as a decision-rights document: explicit build and test commands, hard constraints, do-not-touch paths, and escalation triggers ('stop and ask before touching auth, migrations, payments, CI'). Keep it short - bloated machine-generated context files reduce task success and raise inference cost.

research_gaps: Anthropic's 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report primary PDF is not publicly hosted; all figures are secondhand and should be attributed rather than asserted.
Faros' 2026 dataset (441% review time, +242.7% incidents/PR) is a different cohort from the 2025 report; do not present the two as a single time series.
No public first-party measurement of the 'manager of agents' role's individual performance - no study yet links a developer's agent-management practice to their career outcomes.
CooperBench, the JetBrains ICSE 2026 telemetry and OpenAI's Codex concurrency numbers were only reachable through secondary write-ups; cite as reported, with the secondary source named.
